questions.prompt: A learner claims: 'A 3-bit counter overflowing is basically the same as it just resetting for no reason.' What's wrong with this claim?
options: Overflow isn't random reset — it's the deterministic result of running out of bits, exactly like a car odometer rolling from 999999 to 000000
Nothing is wrong, overflow really is a random reset
Overflow only happens if you press a reset button
3-bit counters can't overflow, only 8-bit ones can
questions.answer: Overflow isn't random reset — it's the deterministic result of running out of bits, exactly like a car odometer rolling from 999999 to 000000
questions.explanation: Wraparound is fully deterministic and predictable: add 1 to the max representable value and it always lands on 0, because there's nowhere else for the carry to go.

questions.prompt: Why does bubble sort's FIRST full pass guarantee the largest element reaches the end, but NOT guarantee the second-largest is in its final place yet?
options: The largest keeps 'winning' every comparison it's in and rides to the end, but the second-largest can still be blocked behind a bigger neighbor mid-pass
It's actually guaranteed after the first pass, all elements settle at once
Bubble sort never guarantees anything about element position
The second-largest also always finishes after one pass
questions.answer: The largest keeps 'winning' every comparison it's in and rides to the end, but the second-largest can still be blocked behind a bigger neighbor mid-pass
questions.explanation: Only one element is guaranteed to fully bubble to its final spot per pass — the current maximum among the unsorted portion. Everything else may need more passes.

questions.prompt: The Stream Comparator halts at the FIRST mismatch and ignores everything after it. Why is this the correct design rather than a limitation?
options: It mirrors the real physical interceptor: once tripped it can't un-trip, so checking further would be simulating something the physical machine can't do
It's a limitation the software should fix by checking the whole stream anyway
It's arbitrary — checking further wouldn't change anything
It only matters for streams longer than 8 items
questions.answer: It mirrors the real physical interceptor: once tripped it can't un-trip, so checking further would be simulating something the physical machine can't do
questions.explanation: Whetstone's rule here is 'zero magic': the code must behave exactly like the physical mechanism it simulates, not add capabilities the marbles-and-gears version doesn't have.

questions.prompt: If you started the 3-bit counter at 0 and want it to return EXACTLY to 0 again, which pulse counts could achieve that?
options: Any multiple of 8 (8, 16, 24, ...)
Any even number
Only exactly 8
Any multiple of 3
questions.explanation: The counter has a period of 8 (2^3 states). It returns to any given value every 8 pulses, so any multiple of 8 pulses brings it back to 0.

questions.prompt: A learner writes a bubble sort that uses Python's built-in `sorted()` function and still passes vec1 and vec3, but fails the AST invariant check. Why does the harness reject it even though the OUTPUT is correct?
options: Because this module's contract requires the comparisons/swaps to be performed step-by-step, not delegated to a library — getting the right answer the 'magic' way defeats the point of the exercise
Because sorted() is slower than bubble sort
Because sorted() only works on numbers, not tokens
The harness doesn't actually check for this
questions.answer: Because this module's contract requires the comparisons/swaps to be performed step-by-step, not delegated to a library — getting the right answer the 'magic' way defeats the point of the exercise
questions.explanation: This is the 'zero-magic' rule running end to end: the SPEC explicitly prohibits shortcuts that skip past the mechanism you're supposed to be learning, even if the final output happens to match.

questions.prompt: Why is it meaningful that the 3-bit counter, the bubble sort, and the stream comparator are all 'pure functions' with no randomness, no clock, no hidden state?
options: It means the exact same input will always produce the exact same output, which is what makes deterministic automated testing possible at all
It means they run faster than non-pure functions
It has no real meaning, it's just a style choice
It means they can't have bugs
questions.answer: It means the exact same input will always produce the exact same output, which is what makes deterministic automated testing possible at all
questions.explanation: Determinism is what lets a fixed set of test vectors catch every bug: if a function could behave differently on the same input, no finite test suite could ever fully verify it.

questions.prompt: A row is already fully sorted before the Token Grid State Machine even starts. Does bubble sort still perform comparisons on it?
options: Yes — it still walks the pointer and compares every neighboring pair, it just never triggers a swap
No — it detects the row is sorted and does nothing
No — sorted rows are skipped entirely by the spec
Only the first comparison happens, then it stops
questions.answer: Yes — it still walks the pointer and compares every neighboring pair, it just never triggers a swap
questions.explanation: This basic version of bubble sort always does the full n(n-1)/2-style comparison sweep regardless of starting order; comparisons and swaps are two separate counts for exactly this reason.

questions.prompt: Two different starting values for the 3-bit counter, say 2 and 6, both receive exactly 8 pulses. Will they end up at the same value?
options: Yes — both return to their own starting value, because 8 pulses is exactly one full period
No — 6 will overflow and 2 won't, so they end up different
Yes — both will always land on 0 regardless of start
It depends on whether the start value is even or odd
questions.answer: Yes — both return to their own starting value, because 8 pulses is exactly one full period
questions.explanation: Since the counter cycles through all 8 states before repeating, adding exactly 8 pulses always returns you to wherever you started, regardless of what that start value was.
